James P. Carse

These passages are translated from the excerpts saved in my Chinese notes, not quoted from the published English edition. Section headings follow the Chinese notes.

## Chapter 1 · There Are at Least Two Kinds of Games, Part I

◆ There are at least two kinds of games. One may be called finite; the other, infinite. A finite game is played to win, while an infinite game is played to keep the game going.

◆ We can therefore say that finite games have temporal boundaries, which all players must agree on. But players must also agree on boundaries of space and number: the game must take place on a defined field with a defined set of participants.

◆ Only one person or team can win a finite game, though the other participants may receive rankings at its end.

◆ Infinite and finite games are alike in one respect only: if players participate, they do so freely. If they must participate, their participation loses its meaning.

◆ In fact, the only purpose of an infinite game is to prevent the game from ending, keeping every participant in play.

◆ Every finite game involves some degree of self-concealment. Players must deliberately forget that participation is voluntary; otherwise, competition and effort will fall away.

◆ With enough practice, we come to believe that we are the people our roles have shaped, and we lead others to believe it too. As Shaw put it, the nature of acting makes us see not this woman as Ophelia, but Ophelia as this woman.

◆ This is true of every role. Someone can enter the role of a mother only voluntarily. Yet the person playing that role must, with the appropriate seriousness, set aside her freedom in order to act as the role requires.

◆ “To believe is to know that one believes, and to know that one believes is not to believe.” —Sartre

If no amount of concealment can hide the concealment itself, the question becomes how seriously we can take this self-concealment, and how far we can go to bring others into the performance with us.

## Chapter 1 · There Are at Least Two Kinds of Games, Part II

◆ A finite game is dramatic only temporarily. Each player wants to make the better outcome inevitable and thereby eliminate the drama. Finite players want to become master players, so technically perfect that nothing can surprise them, so thoroughly trained that they can foresee every move from the outset. The true master plays as though the game were already over, following a script whose every detail is known before the action takes place.

◆ Infinite play is paradoxical, just as finite play is contradictory. The infinite player's purpose is to continue play, not to play for oneself. The contradiction of finite play is that players seek to end the game for their own sake. The paradox of infinite play is that players want others to continue. Only by letting others keep playing can they continue themselves.

Infinite players perform best when they have the least influence over whether the game will continue. That is why they enter it as mortals.

The joy and laughter of infinite play come from trying to begin something we cannot end.

◆ Power is determined by the outcome of a game. A person does not win because they are powerful; they become powerful by winning. If someone already had enough power to win before the game began, what followed would not be a game at all.

◆ A person can possess power only through a recognized title, through the ritual respect of others. Power is never one's own. From this perspective, it reveals the contradiction inherent in every finite game: I can possess power only by stopping play, by showing that the game is over. I can therefore have only the power others give me. Power is conferred by the audience after the game has ended.

Power is contradictory and scripted.

◆ Strength is contradictory. I have strength not because the outcome of competing with others allows me to force them to do what I want, but because I can allow them to do what they want while competing with me.
